title: Writing icons
hook: iconographers pray and fast as they paint

segments.voice: Yesterday, cross and crucifix: one holds the death in view, the other the morning after. Your line was he died, he rose.

A small room, early morning. A wooden board, coated smooth and white. Beside it, jars of colored powder, an egg, a cup of water, brushes. The painter hasn't eaten breakfast, and won't until the day's work is done. Before touching a brush, they stand, make the sign of the cross, and pray. Then they begin, not with a blank idea, but with a pattern handed down for this exact face. One line, then another. The finished face will hang in a church or a home, with candles lit before it. Orthodox Christians have a particular word for this. They don't always call it painting.
screen: `A WHITE BOARD, AN EGG, A CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Some Orthodox Christians speak of writing an icon rather than painting one, because an icon is read, like a page. Its faces, hands, colors and gestures follow patterns passed down from earlier icons, so the iconographer isn't inventing a new look for a saint. They're copying a text faithfully, the way a scribe copies a Gospel: handing something on, not showing off a style. Next, the prayer. Tradition says the iconographer prays before and during the work, and some keep a fast. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his listeners to fast quietly, not for show. An icon is made in that spirit, traditionally without a signature: the hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Then, why pictures at all. Back in year three, the icon wars turned on this. Orthodox Christians point to John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Once God has a human face, that face can be painted. Some Protestant churches keep their walls bare, reading the commandment in Exodus: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Each side takes that text seriously, and reads it differently. Last, the craftsman. In Exodus, God names an artisan, Bezalel: "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Skill with the hands, counted as a gift of the spirit. Iconographers stand in that line.
screen: `AN ICON IS READ, LIKE A PAGE.`

segments.voice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, draw one simple thing in front of you, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, so slowly that each line takes a full breath, with no erasing and no judging. The point is attention, not a good drawing. If you pray, you can pray before the first line, the way an iconographer does; if you don't, let the slowness itself be the practice.
Writing icons. Making a holy image in prayer and fasting, following patterns handed down, so it can be read like a page.
Your line: painting as prayer. The hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, iconographers traditionally pray before and during their work, may keep a fast, and follow patterns handed down for each saint; the finished icons are blessed and placed in churches and homes for prayer.

fork.setup: you're an iconographer, about to begin a face of Christ on a fresh white board. how do you start?
options: sketch freely, in your own new style.
pray, and follow the pattern handed down.
copy a photograph of a model.
fork.reveal: tradition says the iconographer prays first and follows the old pattern. the aim is to hand something on faithfully, not to invent.

chat.says: Why do some people say they 'write' an icon instead of painting it?
options: Because an icon is read like a page: it follows handed-down patterns, made in prayer.
Because icons are mostly words, with a saint's whole life story written across the board.
Because each painter invents a fresh new look for the saint, the way an author writes.
chat.meaning: An icon follows patterns passed down from earlier icons, copied faithfully the way a scribe copies a Gospel, and is made with prayer.
